summary: Samoa is one of the most open countries in the world: visitors of every nationality are issued a free 90-day entry permit on arrival, with no visa and no online authorisation to arrange, provided you hold onward travel and somewhere to stay.

primarySources.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

vaccinations.name: Measles (MMR)
vaccinations.text: Following the 2019 measles epidemic, Samoa strongly encourages travellers to be fully vaccinated against measles, and health screening has been applied at the border at times of outbreak. Carry your vaccination record.

source.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not required for entry, but medical facilities outside Apia are basic and serious cases are flown to New Zealand — cover including medical evacuation is strongly recommended.

source.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

onwardTicket.text: The free 90-day entry permit is granted on the condition that you hold a confirmed onward or return ticket; airlines check this before boarding.

source.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published, but immigration officers expect you to name accommodation for the start of your stay and may ask how you will support yourself.

declarations.name: Samoa arrival card and customs/biosecurity declaration
declarations.submitWindow: Completed on the aircraft or at Faleolo International Airport on arrival
declarations.text: A paper arrival card and a combined customs, biosecurity and health declaration are handed out on the inbound flight. Declare all food, plant and animal products — quarantine officers inspect bags and fines apply for undeclared items.

source.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

currencyLimits.text: Cash of WST 20,000 or more, or the foreign-currency equivalent, must be declared on arrival and departure.

source.name: Samoa Immigration — Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

notes: Biosecurity is strict — fresh fruit, vegetables, seeds, plants, meat and dairy are restricted, and used hiking or camping gear may be inspected and cleaned.
Duty-free allowances for alcohol and tobacco are modest and enforced at Faleolo.
Firearms, ammunition and offensive weapons are prohibited without prior permission from the police.

payments.text: Hotels, resorts and larger shops in Apia take cards, but markets, buses, beach fales and village stalls are cash only. ATMs are plentiful in Apia and scarce elsewhere — draw tālā before heading to Savai'i or the south coast.

safety.text: Samoa is calm and welcoming, with low levels of violent crime. The usual issues are petty theft from open fales and vehicles, strong ocean currents and reef cuts, and driving hazards — narrow roads, roaming dogs and pigs, and driving on the left since 2009.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Samoa travel information

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to October is the dry season — cooler, less humid and outside the November-to-April cyclone and rain period.

tips.text: Sunday is genuinely a day of rest — most shops close and villages hold services. In the early evening many villages observe sa, a short curfew for prayer: if you are driving or walking through and hear the bell or conch, stop and wait quietly until it ends.

Cover shoulders and knees away from resorts, take your shoes off before entering a fale, and never stand and talk over seated people. Beaches usually belong to a village and a small custom fee is normal.

Samoa switched to driving on the left in 2009, so many rental cars are still left-hand drive. Roads are narrow with pedestrians, dogs and pigs, and a local driving permit is required — your rental agency arranges it.
Carry tālā in small notes once you leave Apia. Beach fales, markets, bus fares and village entry fees are cash, and ATMs on Savai'i are few and sometimes empty.
November to April is cyclone season, with heavy rain and occasional flooding. Travel insurance that covers weather disruption is worth having if you visit then.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Samoa?
faq.answer: No. Samoa gives citizens of every country a free visitor entry permit on arrival, valid for up to 90 days. There is nothing to apply for in advance — just arrive with a passport valid six months, a confirmed onward ticket and details of where you are staying.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Samoa?
faq.answer: The entry permit is issued for up to 90 days. If you want to stay longer, the Immigration Division in Apia can extend it — apply before the permit expires and expect to pay a fee of roughly WST 100 per extension.

faq.question: Do I need a return ticket to enter Samoa?
faq.answer: Yes. The free permit is conditional on holding a confirmed onward or return ticket, and airlines check it at check-in. You should also be able to name accommodation for at least the first part of your stay.

faq.question: What vaccinations do I need for Samoa?
faq.answer: Only a yellow fever certificate, and only if you arrive from or have transited a yellow fever risk country. Samoa strongly encourages measles (MMR) vaccination after the 2019 epidemic, and dengue occurs, so mosquito precautions are sensible.

faq.question: Can I visit American Samoa on the same trip?
faq.answer: American Samoa is a separate US territory with its own rules — Samoa's 90-day permit does not cover it. Most nationalities need an entry permit or US visa arranged in advance for American Samoa, so check before booking the short flight or ferry from Apia.
